newsitem.title: ITALY: UN food summit ends under shadow of disagreements.
newsitem.headline: UN food summit ends under shadow of disagreements.

text.p: A U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit ended on Sunday in ringing calls to rid the planet of hunger but with differences over how go about it highlighted by U.S. insistence that it did not recognise a "right to food".

The five-day gathering at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), overshadowed by the refugee crisis in Zaire, was the highest level meeting of its kind called to discuss efforts to end starvation.
It adopted a Declaration on World Food Security and Plan of Action which pledged to halve the number of hungry people from the current 840 million by the year 2015.

"If it depended on me, I certainly would not have set an objective whereby 400 million people continue not to have access to adequate food," FAO's director general Jacques Diouf told a news conference disrupted by protesters shouting "farce".

Diouf said the summit texts, which are non-binding and contain no hard cash commitments, represented a consensus among 186 states which negotiated them. "Arriving at a consensus means a spirit of give and take," said Diouf, from Senegal.

A handful of activists protesting that the summit was an empty gesture came within a few steps of Cuban President Fidel Castro and other leaders on the podium and scuffled with security officials before they were ejected.
Castro, star of the meeting in a field depleted by the absence of most leaders of rich countries, used a speech on Saturday to blame capitalism for world hunger.
He called the summit aims shamefully modest and said on Sunday that the 2015 goal was "the very minimum" to hope for.
"The situation in the world is not improving. Indeed, it is getting worse," the veteran revolutionary said.
He called the U.S. economic blockade of his country "attempted genocide" but said he hoped President Bill Clinton would act to ease it following his re-election this month.

The summit texts were adopted by acclamation at the start of the gathering after more than two years of negotiation and contain compromise language in contentious areas such as trade, development aid, population, sanctions and women's rights.
In a sign of abiding fundamental differences, 15 delegations lodged reservations or interpretations on the texts, including the United States, the world's biggest single food aid provider.

It noted that it had not agreed to a target of spending 0.7 percent of annual economic wealth on development aid and took issue with a reaffirmation by the summit of the "right of everyone to have access to safe and nutritious food".

"The United States believes that the attainment of any "right to adequate food' or "fundamental right to be free from hunger' is a goal or aspiration to be realised progressively that does not give rise to any international obligations nor diminish the responsibilities of national governments toward their citizens," the U.S. statement said.

Washington, which led rich nations in calls in Rome to make free trade the key to ending the poverty at the root of hunger, fears recognition of a "right to food" could lead to lawsuits from poor nations seeking aid and special trade provisions.

Neither Clinton nor the leaders of most other industrialised nations took part in the summit, which fell far short of Diouf's stated aim of bringing together some 100 of the world's heads of state and government.
"That was not a particularly comforting thing," South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told reporters.

Non-governmental organisations (NGO) which met on the sidelines of the summit voiced dissatisfaction with the action plan, telling a news conference that leaders had missed an opportunity to make meaningful commitments.

An NGO representative, Jeanot Minla Mfou'ou of Cameroon, told the closing summit session that the world had to choose between "profit for a few or food for all". "Food is a fundamental and unquestionable human right," he said.
The summit was the last in a series of major U.N. conferences over the past four years to map out an agenda for tackling the world's problems on the eve of the 21st century.

Diouf was adamant at the outset that the food summit should not re-open wounds on sensitive issues such as how to manage a booming population, the cause of a bitter row between the Vatican and Washington in 1994 at a U.N. conference in Cairo.

The Vatican was joined by several delegations in Rome, including Argentina and many Moslem states, in reaffirming objections to language on population and family planning in the food summit documents, which echo the Cairo agreement.
